From the London Times, January 15, 1840. UNITED STATES BANK. The following correspondence has been published : þÿ (Copy.) " Bishopsgate-street, Dec. 31, 1839. " S. Jaudon, Esq. " Dear þÿSir, We have only awaited your return to this country to call your pointed attention to an article which appeared in The Times newspaper of this place of the 24th inst., headed " American Affairs," and signed A Genevese Traveller," with statements designed to be injurious to our chaiacter, and of we feel that some notice must be taken such calumnies, because, if the reports there mentioned were really current in the United States, they must have come to the cognizance of the President of the United States Bank, and those connected with the institu. tion ; and, if uncontradicted in any way by them, must have received their tacit sanction whilst by their communication from you, and the recent visit of Mr. Aisop to this country, they must have known that such insinuations were entirely without foundation We can ourselves have no objection to a lull publication of all our correspondence and transactions with vou and with the bank, but we do not wish it without your consent, nor should we publish, except in self defence, negotiations which appear to us only to interest the United States Bank and ourselves " We have never hesitated to declare fully and frankly to you our objections to the system which that bank has pursued, and which, in our opinion, has led to the difficulties in which that institution and vourselt have been latterly involved, as well as our determina-

tion not to appear, either as agents or loanm ikers for the Bank, as long as that system was continued ; but we have always been very ready, consistently with our principles and proper prudence, to co operate with you in averting the calamity which would have resulted from your failure in meeting your engagements in this country. We need not repeat the charges against us which the article referred to contains, for they are sufficiently known to you; and we should have supposed that you yourself would have been anxious to refute snch calumnies against those who have assisted you ; but if vou feel any objection to such a step, we must, in justice to ourselves, distinctly ask you whether our conduct towards you has at anv time been marked by a breach of confidence, gross deception, or perfidy, and whether the statement in the article concerning us and Mr. Bates individually is or is not false 7 " We do not fear any bad effects which such insinuations against our character might produce here, or anywhere where we are known, but, if these reports arc connived at by those who best know their falsehood, we feel that we most be prepared to meet them by aa explicit denial. " We remain trulv. dear Sir, " Your obedient servants, "BARING BROTHERS an CO"
(Copy.) "Messrs- Baring Brothers, and Co. "Dear Sirs, þÿ 1 have received your commimieation of bis mominrr relative in the ar-

ticle which appeared in 'Ike Times newspaper of the 24th instant, signed A Genevese ' Traveller.' Just at the moment I was leaving Paris 1 saw that letter for the first time, and glanced very hastily over it, but did not again see it or hear of it until you read it to me yesterday, and having been myself the subject of repeated attacks in the same newspaper, which 1 have passed by with silent contempt, 1 should not have thought of noticing the letter in question had you not called my attention specially to it. " 1 can have no hesitation in saying to you what I have taken pleasure in stating very frequently to others, that the conduct of your house towards me personally has uniformly evinced the most friendly disposition; and that 1 have repeatedly received from you important and valuable aid in my arrangements to meet my heavy engagements for the Bank of the United States. " In the particular transaction alluded to, so far from having acted with ' gross deception and perfidy in refusing to do on the 23d of August last what you had previously agreed to do, which was to unite with other friends in a large purchase of state stocks, or advances upou them, you not only punctually and cheerfully performed your engagement, : but I lind on reference to mv letter id' that ' date to the President of the Bank of the United States that 1 mentioned to him my consultations with you about the proposed arrangement, and expressed the opinion that 1 could not fail to accomplish it.

" As to the other part of the charge in that letter þÿ viz, that Mr. Bates sent out by the steamer of the 24th August a list of my payables, with a declaration that the bank must fail on the 20th. and that these were used for the purpose of stock -gambling, 1 need only say that although you may have considered it right to send such a list, yet I am quite sure (whatever others may or may' not have done, of which I know nothing) your house is entirely incapable of using any confidential information for any unworthy purpose. " in regard to the Bank of the United States, I may add that although from its anxicty to aid other banks, and its desire to assist the states l»y advances upou their stocks, it mav have stepped out of its usual course of banking, yet 1 consider this but a temporary departure from its regular and fixed principles ; and the special circumstances which were thought to justify this departure having ceased to exist, the bank is now pursuing, and I am confident will continue to pursue, that svstem which placed it heretofore on the pinnacle ofcredit. " 1 am, with great regard, your obd't. serv't. " S. JAUDON. " London. Dec. 31, 1839."

Tub Great Western þÿ We are happy in being able to say that the examination of this noble- vessel since her laving up shows that there is neither spot nor blemish in her, and that she does not require caulking or coppering, beyond a lew sheets to replace those which have been rubbed off by the coal vessels, or have been removed for the purpose of a thorough examination Ail the paitsof the engines which are not fixtures have been taken out and thoroughly examined, and are now in progress of replacement The pla. of the directors is to overhaul her completely once a year, and we should say after 35,000 nautical miles steaming per annum, it is an almost indispensable one, if confidence is to be maintained with the public. gineers, stokers, and servants, whose berths below were a great inconvenience and annoyance to the fore cabin passengers, are to be accommodated on deck ; also that the lares are to be all eq :al in the fore and after accommodation, the lore state rooms hating been considerably enlarged. WKBBBB (From the Hombay Ornette of January 29.) It has been determined by the Governor General that a large amount of tonnage shall be immediately taken up for the conveyance of troops to China, and that, in addition to the land forces about to be transported to tbe celestial empire, the co operation of all the vessels of war in the eastern seas shall be given towards the reduction of the pride of the Chinese. The Druid, 44 guns. Lord Churchill, is under orders to proceed to China direct, after landing Captain Hobson, the Governor of Netv Zealand, at his destination.

We have long enough borne the brunt of insult from the Chinese authorities, and it is now destined, after a long period of suffering on our par', that there shall be a bloody termination of tbe conflict. Let t he Chinese remember, or rather reflect, that 20 ships of war and ten gallant regiments are hardly to be irifl .d with, and gram concessions in time, or China rutty ere long become as much a Biitish province as India is at present. Only imagine the brother to the Sun and Moon a pensioner on our government for ball a million a-year. with a British ministry to manage his affairs ! Where would then be tbe vaunting commission intrusted to Lin, and where the prohibitions to British commerce at the port of Canton ? We are happy that matters in regard to China have taken this cheering turn, and hope all will turn out for the best. The island of Sapata, about to he taken possession of by our troops is situated about 100 miles from the coast of Cuchin Chinn, and although not so near the scene of hostilities as we could have wished, is yet admirably adapted for most of the purposes of a maritime depot, from which troops can easily be conveyed according to the exigencies of the occasion to any point upon which their services may he required. It will, of course, lie only a starting post from which we shall enter a more enlarged sphere of conquest; and when our ships of war, as well as the vessels conveying the regiments from Calcutta, appear in the China Seas, for tiie protection of our

trade and the vindication of our honour, wo he to the devoted cities of the coast, wo he to the degraded Commissioner Lin, and direful destruction to the celestial empire, which will shake with the report of ottr cannon to its very centre! A war of defence has ever been, where Britain is concerned, a war of conquest The former was the foundation upon which the superstructure of our Indian empire has been reared, and it will he the groundwork of our ascendancy in a new quarter of the globe.

The Cyclops, War Steamer. þÿ On Monday' the Cyclops, war steamer, left the river for Portsmouth, having tak«n in from Woolwich, a quantity of stores, ammunition &c , and 22 marines, under the command of a lieutenant. She is the largest steamer in the British navy, and has two engines of 150 horse power each, with a crew of stokers, engineers, and mariners, of 260 men ; she is commanded by Captain Austin, late of the Medea and it is said her destination is China It is supposed she will take in soldiers and complete her store at Portsmouth, as Sir Charles Grey, who visited her in llte river last week, took great

pains to satisfy himself of her capabilities in this respect, her lower deck being proved to his satisfaction, by Capt. Austin, tube adequate to the accommodation of 1,000 men for a short voyage, and for at least 300 to India.

From tile New York Commercial Advertiser, April 7, 1840. Tub Halifax Stbamkks þÿ We have seen various accounts of the probable time when Mr. Cunard's line of steam packets will commence their trips. Some say it will he tins month, while others mention a period as late as the middle of June. From the best information we ean obtain we understand that the first of the new boats will start about the 1st of June þÿ that will he the Britannia. There are to he four boats to from the line, the Britannia, Caledonia, Columbia and Arcadia. Mr. Cunard's contract was to commence on the 1st of May, but it is presumed he will not he bound strictly to a lew days, when it is known that he is making every exertion to complete his boats. Should tiie British government insist on the strict performance of the contract, as to the time of departure from England, steamers will he chartered to do the service until the Britannia is in readiness to take her place in the line. Mr Cunard has purchased the steam packet Unicorn, about the dimensions of the Sirius. This vessel was to leave England the 1st of May lor Halifax She is intended to run between Piotou and (.Quebec, and will probably bring out the hist direct mail for the provinces.

Mortality \ mono si gueiial officers in tub British Army --From an article in the London Morning Post, we learn that ineie have died in the British army since the brevet of 1837, no less than ninety general officers, viz: One field marshal, tinny two generals, thirty seven lieutenant generals, and twenty major-generals, whose name are given. The average age of three hundred and fifty generals, still in service, is said to exceed seventy-five years, from which we might infer that the hardships and privations of military life rather tend to increase than shorten tiie days of army officers. When they arrive at a certain age, with sound constitutions, the chances ol attaining gieater a age are probably equal to those ol any other profession It is wiih the young, no doubt, whose duties require them to he much exposed in unhealthy climates, that the mortality is greatest. His Majesty enumerates ail the improvements made in the Government since his accession. Among these is the extinction of the whole of the foreign and a great part of the home debt ; an increase of the pro tin of the bank from 248,000 thaiets banco to 700,000 ; the formation of art army of 100.099 effective men ; the creation of a coast guild of 250 gun boats; an augmentation of the fleet ; an increase of commerce and manufactories and general industry ; and. finally, a perfect union between Sweden and Norway, which had previously been divided by a mutual spirit of animosity. Expedition to China. þÿ We are enabled to lay before our readersjthis week a correct statement of the particulars of the vessels which have already sailed, and are yet to ail, for the purpose of vindicating British1 honour on the coast of China. The Blenheim, 74 guns, sailed direct for China from Portsmouth, 17th February; Melville, 74 guns, from the Cape; Wellesley, 74 guns, from the Indian station ; Blonde, 46, direct from Plymouth, 26th February ; Druid, 48, from the Cape via Sydney, 5th November ; Pvlades, 18, direct from Plymouth, on the 23d Feb; Nimrod, 20, from Plymouth, on 24th Feb. (with duplicate instructions for Admiral Elliot) ; Modeste, 18, from the Cape, 5lh Nov ; Wanderer, 18, sailed for the Cape, 12th Feb , from Plymouth, with orders to Admiral Elliot to proceed with all his corvettes and take the command in China. Besides these ships, another 74 has been dispatched. At Portsmouth there are now waiting orders, the Pique, 38 ; Andromache, 28 ; 10 vessels from the Indian station, from 18 to 28 guns each, part of the Indian navy ; 2 vessels from the Cape station, 18 guns each ; 2 from the South American station, 18 and 28 guns each ; 2 from the New South Wales station, 18 to 28 guns each ; 2 large steamer supposed to be the Sesostris and Queen. þÿ Commercial Journal.

From the St. James's Chronicle , March 28. TRIUMPH OP THE THIERS MINISTRY. An extraordinary express from Paris received this morning announces a more brilliant triumph for M. Thiers than either he or his most sanguine friends could have anticipated. The first vote on M. þÿD Angervillc's amendment, for reducing the secret service grant by 100,000 francs, was decided at half-past five on Thursday. The numbers were : þÿ Total number present, 419. For the amendment 158 Against it 261 Majority for the Ministers 103 The subsequent division on the general question was as follows : For the bill 246 Against it 100 Majority for the Ministers 80 The result of this contest is regarded in France as of great importance, as it regards the relations of France with England, and the peace of Europe generally. deeper sense of the imot lance of the English , alliance than he has had credit for. And if ) his notions on the Eastern Questiou have j really undergone no change, it need no longer be a source ol jealousy and bickering to the Five Powers.

WUrni The intelligence received from the East In lies by the due overland mails is highly interesting in other than a political point of view. The statistical details which have reached us of the exportation of the produets ot India, alt »rd most ample proof that that vast country is rapidly advancing in coin mercial prosperity, notwithstanding the restrictions wmch are still imposed upon importation thence into Great Britain. Those most anxious to promote the prosperity of India anticipate that before many years have elapsed the manufacturers of Great Britain will he enabled to obtain a large proportion of the cotton they require from that country, thus rendering them less dependent than they are at present for supplies of the staple upon America; that tobacco will be raised in abundance : and that the Chinese may be compelled to acknowledge and protect the British trade with them, when they find that the þÿ þÿBarbarians can obtain tea in abundance from Upper Assam. It is impossible to estimate the advantages which must result to the manufacturers of the United Kingdom, by the accomplishment of these great objects. The demand for British manufacturers in India must be increased an hundred fold could lhat colony so far extend her cultivation of cotton, tobacco, sugar, and tea, as to render us less dependent on foreign countries lor these leading articles of commerce.

Anatomy. þÿ Dr. Bedford, of this city, has lately imported from France a most ingenious specimen of human anatomy, artificially constructed of the material familiarly known as papier much'1. It consists of a perfect model of man, nearly six feet high, standing upon a pedestal, and presenting the appearance of the entire body, divested of the skin and cellular tissue. The muscles, blood vessels and nerves on the whole surface are exposed, and are all beautifully colored to the life, as indeed is every portion of this admirable contrivance. Each particular muscle, artery, vein, nerve, and indeed the most minute portion of the organization, is capable of being successively removed, until hundreds of pieces are detached for separate examination, and the whole edifice of the human body is thus literally taken down, and its multiplied portions contemplated apart, as well as in their natural and relative positions. And þÿ alter the head, trunk and extremities, together with all the internal organs, are thus separately laid upon the tables, and even their internal and external organization exposed in detached parts, so ingenious and accurate is the adaptation of all these distinct portions of human structure to each other, that in a few minutes every portion can be restored to its proper place, and the entire body be thus reconstructed as before. Anatomy may thus be studied both by analysis and synthesis, the entire body, with all its organs, being first taken apart, with as

much ease as the fragments of a dissected map; and then every portion may be restored to its place, until the whole is as perfect as before. But the grand and important advantage of such a model is in the facility it affords lor cultivating the study of human anatomy, without the use of a human body, and without inhaling the pucrescent atmosphere of a dissecting room which the nun-professional know how to estimate.

!»"&$' '&'& Au exhibition of this magnincent work of art was given by Dr. Beufotd a few days since, in the presence of a latge number oi gentlemen, among whom we recognized many of the most respectable physicians and surgeons of this city, and ail of whom expressed their high gratification that so valuable an acquisition to anatomical pursuits had been introduced into our city, arid all were delighted with the accuracy and beauty of the mechanism by which the various parts of this complicated structure can be so readily removed and replaced. Dr. B. intends employing it for teaching anatomy as we learn, to popular classes; and at the same time, with commendable liberality, he extends to all his professional brethren the privilege of examining it at their leisure, which will extend its usefulness. We marvel that our colleges have not long since procured similar means of instruction, and that our city has to be indebted to individual enterprize for this method of teaching the all important science of anatomy. þÿ New York Commercial Advertiser, April 3.

TUB ROYAL SOCIETY OF NORTHERN ANTIQUARIES at Copenhagen held its fifteenth annual meeting on the 3 Oth January last. þÿ Its new President, His Excellency Prime Minister of State Masting opened the proceedings with a short address, which he introduced as follows : I am deeply sensible of the Honor the Society has conferred upon me by electing me its President, although I acknowledge my inability to be to the Society what my Honorable Predecessor was, a man whose celebrity is grounded on the just claim of his erudition. 1 shall however, supported by the Societys scientific and meritorious men who stand by my side make it my aim to be found worthy of the place, assigned to me by a Society whose most distinguished men exhibit a zealous co-operation, and whose exertions have found acknowlegement, not alone in this part of the Earth we belong to, but also beyond the Atlantic, in that other Hemisphere, to which our bold Ancestors extended their exploits and w here it has been the good fortune of our Society to raise to them a worthy and lasting memorial. It is gratifying to see how the great remembrances of the antient times of the North, thus more and more induce awakened observation ; also how their numbers increase who devote their attention to that land of our old History's preservation, to that remarkable Rocky island far in the North Sea, where the old danish tongue through centuries to our time, has been cherished and preserved unchanged. Having reminded the Society of the nume-

rous and valuable tokens of favor and regard it had received from our departed Monarch King Frederik the VI, he announced that His Majesty King Christian the VIII, who already by many antiquarian communications had earlier given the Society proofs of his interest in its objects, had in the most gracious manner declared the continuance of his favor and protection. The Secretary afterwards gave an account of the State of the Society and its proceeding during the past year 1839. The Society had that year published four new volumes namely þÿ Scripta Historica Islandorum vol. Vllland þÿIX

þÿ Historiske Fortiellinger om Islaendernes Fserd hjemme og þÿude or Historical accounts regarding the transactions of the Icelanders at home and abroad 1st vol. also a volume of þÿ Annaler for Nordisk þÿOldkyndighed, or annals regarding Northern Antiquities which will be more particularly noticed at another lime. Several communications enriching the knowledge of antient times, were received for the societys annals and memoirs of which the following are mentioned viz : From Professor Kruse communicating an extensive account of a great Antiquarian journey undertaken by him at the Emperors command in the Russian þÿEmpire E s ast Sea provinces Lifland, Esthland and Courlond ; the main object of which was to trace with what nations these provinces in old times had stood in connection, and the important results of which he explains. It is hereby seen that Scandinavian Antiquities are found in abundance, especially along the Sea Coast, and Ranks of the larger Rivers, and that numerous objects brought from thence, which serve for comparison with our Northern

Occasioned by the work þÿ Antiquitates Americana;, Mr. Aubin in Mexico, bad in a þÿ letter to the President of the Society made a communication of great interest, containing an extract of Mexican old Manuscripts as a confirmation from undoubted facts in reference to Mexico, that in more parts o America, there had been a white population, before Columbus discovered this part of the world ; and that they have found traces of Christianity long before the arrival of the Spaniards. Her þÿMajesty Packet s Crane, after an unusually short passage, twenty days, þÿ þÿ arrived at Barbados on the 23d ultimo. The second April mails for these islands were brought by this conveyance and those for this island were landed here <>n Thursday morning last. A dearth of news characterises the files through which we have waded. Intelligence of the happiness ol the domestic circle at the Royal Palace is always most pleasing, and that is recorded in every print before us The political movements in the Imperial Parliament have been of little importance to the colonial reader. Lord John Russell had introduced a bill for the re union of the two Canadas, and have laid on the table of the House a bill concerning the Clergy Reserves in those provinces. This latter would remain on the table during a period prescribed by Act of Parliament, (30 days,) and will at the end ol that time become a law, if no sufficient opposition be raised

þÿ him of þÿExeter at their head; but the right Rev. prelate had been so sermonised by Lord Meibom ne, that it is doubted whether he will again come to the scratch. The Archbishop of Canterbury had given notice of his intention to move an address to the Queen, praying her Majesty to withhold the Royal assent. The meritorious services of Sir John Colborne, (now Lord Seaton) in Canada, have been rewarded by her Majesty with a pension of £2,000 a year, to be enjoyed by himself and his two successors. The Paris papers mention that a strong sensation was created in the French capital by the receipt, on Saturday, of letters from Leghorn, announcing the prospect of an immediate rupture between Great Britain and Naples ! According to this statement the British minister having called upon the King of Naples with a note in reference to the sulphur question, that magnificent potentate was pleased to tear it in pieces, and throw it on the ground ; a piece of impertinence which was followed by the demand on the part of our minister of his passports, A letter from Messina, dated March 19, on the subject of the reported dispute, asserts that our minister at Naples distinctly informed the King, that if the contract was not rescinded, and the proposed indemnity paid, he had instructions to call for the assistance of the Btilish vessels of war at Malta. This announcement, it is said, so enraged his Majesty, that he ordered that immediate arrangements should be made in every part of in dominions.

From the New York Commercial Adoertieer, March 4. 1840. Correspondence of Commercial Advertiser Constantinople, Dec. 11, 1839. 1 send you one of the most remarkable productions of modern times, considering its origin. It is not a constitution, but it approaches nearer to one than any thing which we had expected to see in this quarter. On the third day of the last month an assembly was convoked at Constantinople at which were present the Grand Seignor the high officers of state, of the army, and of religion, representatives from the embassies of foreign powers, and the patriarchs aud heads of the several Christian sects. Prince Joinvilfe, a son of the French King, then at Constantinople, was also present, /falil Pasha, the Feraskier, (commander in chief) then read, in the name of the Sultan, tiie following hatti scheriff, which is hereafter to be the fundamental law of the Ottoman Empire. The translation I have made from the Greek. þÿ Hatti Sclieriff. þÿ The whole world knows that during the earlier periods ol the Ottoman monarchy, the commands of the glorious Koran and the laws of the empire were universally respected, and in consequence the government increased in majesty and power, and the subjects, without exception, enjoyed a great degree tranquili- of ty and prosperity. During the last one hundred and fifty years, however, on account of a succession of misfortunes of various kinds, the people have disregarded the sacred code of laws and regulations, and the result has been that the internal strength and prosperity

of the empire have given way to weakness Hid poverty. Thus it is, every state loses its stanility when it ceases to respect its laws. These considerations have continually oecuined our tiu>,jghts; and since the day luat we ascended the throne, our only desire i, is been the public good and the improvement of the condition of the provinces, and the relief of the people. Whoever considers the geographical situation of the Ottoman provinces, the fertility of the soil, and the industrious habits of the popu1 ition, must be convinced that under a proper administration a m >st happy result (which bv divine aid we hope obtain) to can be brought about in a few years. Full therefore of confidence that we shall have the help of the Most /figh, especially when sustained by the intercession of our Prophet, (Mohammed), we have determined to give to the provinces, which compose the Ottoman Empire, the benefits of a good administration. þÿ These institutions have reference princi. pally to thuse three points : 1st. Security for the life, reputation and properly of our subjects þÿ 2d. Regularity in the mode of assessing and raising þÿtaxes and 3d. Regularity in levying soldiers, and determining their time of service. 1st. Life and reputation; arc not these indeed the most precious of possessions ? þÿ What man is there, however much he may dislike a resort to violence, who will not n- vertheless resort to it, to the injury of the government and his country, when his life and reputation are in danger 1 On the other
hand, if he enjoys perfect security in these

»AST33S þÿ »»8!Tr»»333S »a<t>BJ»3Um©e ATBS, respects, he will never swerve from the path of loyalty, and all his actions will have reference to the welfare of the state and the good of his fellow subjects. þÿ If the citizen has no security for his property, he becomes regardless of the voice of his rulers and his country. Occupied solely with the difficulties which encompass his own path, he never spends a thought upon the public weal. On the contrary, if his possessions, of what ever kind they may be, are perfectly secured to him by the laws, then, earnestly engaged in his own business, (the sphere of which he endeavors to extend, in order that he may extend that of his enjoyments,) he finds his love for his rulers aud his country, and his spirit of devotion to their interests, daily increasing. 2d. In regard to taxes and imposts ; it is of all importance that this suoject be placed on its proper looting, inasmuch as the government, which is compelled, lor the Uelenee of its territory, to be at large expenses for the support of armies, <fcc , has no other mode of obtaining the necessary funds, except by levying contributions upon its subjects. þÿ Although, by divine favor, our subjects have for some time been delivered from the scourge of monopolies, winch were once strangely enough considered as a source of revenue, there yet exists a most destructive custom ; (called lltizam,) according to which our provinces are venal. Under this system the administration, both civil ami financial, of a particular territory, is committed into the hands

ofa single individual, oltenlnues of the most violent and avaricious passions, who has no rule of action but his own selfishness. þÿ is It necessary, therefore, lor the future, that each subject of the Ottoman empire be regularly taxed, according to his power and wealth. Nothing larther is to be exacted þÿ It is important, also, that laws be framed limiting the expenditures of the army, both on land and at sea. þÿ 3d Alihough, as we have said before, the defence of the country is an all important object, and consequently it is the duty of the inhabitants to furnish soldiers for this end, yet it is equally necessary that laws be enacted fixing the number which each town or province is to furnish according to the !i»Cc9' sities of the moment, and limiting the term or service to four or five years For it is manifestly unjust, and at the same tune destructive to the interests of agriculture and industry, to levy without regard to the differences of population, a larger number in some places, and a smaller number in others, than they are able or ought to furnish. The result of such a system is to drive the soldiers to despair, and to depopulate the country, by retaining them for life in the service. þÿ In a word, without these different laws, the necessity of which every body feels, the government must remain without strength, without wealth, without prosperity, without tranquility. By means of them, we may expect all these blessings. þÿ For the future, the trial of all accused

persons shall be public, in accordance with our divine law ; and there shall always be due inquiry and examination into their guilt, and without regular trial and condemnation, no individual shall he allowed either secretly or openly to destroy another by poison or by anv other means. þÿ It shall not be lawful for any one to attack the character of another.

þÿ Every individual shall have the quiet possession of his property, of whatever kind, and shall be at liberty to dispose of it as he will, without V hindrance from another. For instance, the innocent heirs of a criminal shall not be deprived of their legal rights; nor shall the property of a criminal be confiscated þÿ These imperial privileges are granted to all our subjects, without exception ; of whatever religion or sect they may he, they shall be equal sharers in them. Perfect security is hereby granted by us to all the inhabitants of the empire for their life, their reputation, and their property, in accordance with the text of our sacred law þÿ As to other p >ints, inasmuch as they ought to be regulated in accordance witn the views of our wisest heads, our Council of Justice (which shall lie augmented in numbers as necessity demands,) to which shall be added, on such days as we shall appoint, our ministers and notables, shall form an assembly for the purpose of framing all laws necessary for securing the rights of life and property, as well as those having reference to the assessment of taxes. Each rrmmbet of the council shall be at liberty to express freely his sentiments, and to give his advice. The laws concerning military service shall he debated in the military council, which shall hold its sessions in the house of the Seraskier, (commander in chief) þÿ When any law is frairn , in order to have force it shall first be present d to us If approved, it shall receive our sanction, which

hall be written at the head of the iaw, with our imperial hand. þÿ As this fundamental law has for its end the reinvigoration of religion, of the government. of the nation, and of the empire, we hereby promise to do nothing contrary to its requirements. As a pledge of our determination thus to act. we shill, after depositing it in the hall where is preserved the mantle of our glorious prophet, in the presence of the .ulemas and grandees of the empire, make oath in the name of God, and then administer the oath to the ulemas and grandees. þÿ Whoever, alter this, of the ulemas or grsndess. or whatever other person, shall violate this law, shall suffer, without regard to his rank or consideration, a corresponding punishment ; and to this end a penal code shall be established þÿ As all the officers o! state receive at present stated salaries, and as we shall hereafter regulate the salaries of other officers who have not been sufficiently rewarded, a severe law shall be passed against bribery and other wicked actions, (Richvetia.) on the part of Government þÿ a thing which the divine law condemns, and which is a pioniinent cause of the weakness of the empire. þÿ The above regulations being a complete renovation of ancient usages, this imperial rescript shall be publicly read in Constantinople, and in all other places in the empire, and copies of it shall be officially communicated to the ambassadors of friend I v powers residing in Constantinople, in order that they may be the witnesses of this grant of institu-

tions, which, if it please God, shall continue to the end of time. þÿ May the most High have us all in his holy keeping. þÿ Whoever shall transgress these laws, let him be the object of the divine curse, and forever he deprived of the least degree of hapþÿpiness.

TUliKFY. It is probable that the above document had its origin with Rescind Pasha and Achmet Fetht Pasha, late ambassadors from the sublime Porte to England and Prance. They returned two or three months since from those courts, and have been long reputed enlightened and liberal minded men for Turks. Every friend of free institutions must sympathise with them in their efforts to establish such institutions in their own country. What success they will have time alone can reveal. If these laws are carried into effect, it is ray settled conviction that the whole system of Mohammedanism will he torn up by the roots. The very genius of that system is opposition to improvement. The Koran itself forbids intercourse with Christian nations. Hence the Turks have never had any foreign commerce Every step in the progress of the late Sultan was in defiance of the principles of his professed religion. The doctrine of this document is religious equality The doctrine of the Koran is death, tribute, or a change of religion, to every conquered Christian. To what a miserable condition is the Ottoman Empiie reduced. In Asia her onlv possessions arc Asia Minor, comprehending a portion of Armenia and Mesopotamia- In Europe, she has Bulgaria, Roumelv and Albania. Of islands she yet retains Cyprus, and those which lie along the Western and Southwestern coasts of Asia Minor. Egypt and Syria, and the islands of Crete, and portions of Arabia are in the hands of Mohammed Ali; Moldavia, Wallachia, Servia

and Bosnia, which formed the Northern portion of European Turkey, are suhstanialiy iodependant of the government at Constantinople. Thus has the Sultan been losing province after province of his once extensive empire. At the same time, the population of the provinces that remain to him has been wasting away. I have travelled considerably in Asia Minor, and from the observations 1 have made. I do not hesitate to give it as my opinion, that there are not in that region above live -millions of inhabitants. It is probable that an accurate census would show a much smaller number. Jivery where one sees the finest tracts of land lying waste, þÿ and towns in ruins or falling to ruin. I was particulailv impressed with the fact that the process of depopulation has gone on to a vast extent, during a tour which I made in some parts of the antient Ionia. I went over that portion whieh contained the cities of Bronchidae, Miletus. Piiene, Pannionium, Ephesus, Colophon, Natium and several others þÿ a region which must have had some hundreds of thousands of souls in its best davs, but which now has not twenty thousand. I have seen but little of European Tnrkev. þÿ Probably the depopulation there has not been as great as in Asia Minor. Perhaps there may be four millions, though I think this is a large estimate, in the provinces which are still subject to the Sultan. If so, then we shall have, say nine millions of souls for the present Ottoman Empire. Nine millions of people under a good ad-

ministration, and occupying a territory so well adapted for agricultural and commercial pursuits as Turkey, might indeed make a strong and rich empire. But in the present case we are to remember that through ages of misgovernment, the monarchy has become

absolutely weak, its resources are exhausted, the habits of a large portion of the people are ad verse kto effort, and the spirit of improvement is stifled by a false religion. Ada to this, that, at the present moment, the government is placed in peculiarly difficult circumstances iu consequence ofhaving neither army nor fleet, the one having been cut off in battle, and the other having gone over to the enemy. The Ottoman Empire can no longer stand without foreign aid. It depends for its very existence on the will of the European powers. If they should simply do nothing all is lost to Turkey. It is the tear of them only which prevents the Pasha of Egypt from going at once to Constantinople, and girding upon his own side, and that without opposition too, the sword of Qthman. Sad as the condition of the people of Turkey is, that of the subjects of Mohammed Ali is far worse. It is questionable whether human nature has reached a lower level, at least on an extended scale, in any other part of the world, than it has among the fellahs of Egypt. 1 have seen nothing like it els« where The population of that fine country, which in ancient times amounted to seven millions, is not now probably one and a half millions. All the young men are dragged away from their homes to fill the ranks of the army, or to labor in the arsenals I observed in the arsenal at Alexandria that the laborers there were market on the hand os a preventive against desertion, being thus compelled to wear a perpetual badge of their slavery.

Our present remarks will be understood as applying to the commerce of our own little loyal istai.d; which is favored very much by its geographical position making it, independently of other great branches of trade, in a measure an entrepot for the supply of our Sister islands þÿ We review as follows in their respective order : BANKS. A new era has arisen in the introduction of a Banking system into the West Indies þÿ & desideratum long wished for, notwithstanding the powerful opposition of many Capitalists residing in the Colonies, who necessarily be came alarmed at the injury it was calculated to effect, ns regarded their interests by the curtailment of their speculations tu exchanges and coins The Colonial Bank led the way. and is formed of parties chiefly residing at London; of very large resources. Jt started wuh a working capital oi £500,000 sterling, and a Royal Charter; but we observe there were very few shares in this establishment reset vi ed lor the Colonies, and however shululiy its operations were commenced iV continued vet there has been always a strong feeling against it, on account of its foreign ownership ; still

it i-.- due to tite late Manager of the branch in this Colony to ol>$t ve, tuat he couducled the business of the institution in a fiist-m d manner, and in a way to silence a gooil oval of prejudice. Now the advantages given by the Colonial Bank for a " const leialion," have b"en many and manifold, and certain it is that a gnat number of traders au<1 ngr ruiturms bit iff been largely served by it wligsa hUnSli lip

!D&rrsx dust rv ami inleitts otherwise would possibly not have been called into action, except through its timely assistance. It is therefore idle, and unfair to rail against an establishment which will carry the many along prosperously, whilst the mischief which it might he supposed to produce by the pecuniary facilities it affords, can oniv extend to patties whose coffers are already sufficiently stored with the riches of the world. We believe a better organized system than that by which tin; branch of the Colonial Hank in this Island is governed, cannot be met with, and that the aggregate of advantages arising from its introduction here is quite equal to any similar concern in other countries. The West India Bank, of a purely local on w net ship, w as in the early part of Match, called into operation; and it bids fair for popularity, and in all probability w ill do a good share of business. The contract with her Majesty's government and this company for the conveyance of the mails to and from the West India Colonies, the Gulf of Mexico, &c., having been signed, we shall endeavour to give our readers some idea of the services to be performed The Duectors of the Company are men of enormous wealth, and of the highest respectability, and deeply interested in the West Indian and American trade. John Irving, Esq, M. I. is Chairman; Andrew Colviile, Esq., Deputy Chairman. Thomas Baring, George Brown, James Cavan, Robert Cotesworth, Henry Davidson, Russell Ellicc, George Hibbert, John Irving, Jun. W. S Marshall, P. M. Stewart, Esquires, are the Directors. The capital of the company is to be £1,500,000 in 1500 shares, of £100. Steamers are to leave England on the 2d and loth of every month for Barbados, making the passage in 16 days; and, after a stay of 10 hours, delivering the mails for Tobago, British Guiana, and Surinam, will proceed to Grenada, making the passage of 140 miles in 12 hours, stopping'12 hours, and landing there the mails and passengers for all the Windward Islands, Ate. The same boat will then proceed to the Havannah, by St. Thomas, Porto Rico. Cape Nichola Mole, St Jago de Cuba, and Jamaica, with the outward mails, and will return froin the Havannah to Samana ( Hay ti) by the same route, with the Inward European and intercolonial mails from these several places, the Gulf of Mexico, the Havannah, and South America; and at Jamaica,

take in the mails collected from the several windward ports, and thence proceed by Turk's Island (there land and take in mails), with all the European mails to England þÿ The whole voyage from England to Havannah, including stoppages at all tire places, will occupy but 27 days þÿ the return passages being made in the same time. Grenada is to be the general depot for coals þÿ and the day before the mails arrive at Barbados from England, a steamer is to leave the former lor the latter Island ; and, having taken in mails, will proceed to Tobaga. Demerara, Berbice and Parimaribo, and return by the same route, leaving Demerara six, Berhice five, and Tobago nine days, to reply to letters from England. Another steamer will proceed from Grenada to Trinidad, Laguayra, Porto Cahello, and Curagoa, doing the distance, including stoppages, in three days. In two days more she passes from Curugoa to Samaria, thence to St. Thomas by Portorico, in a day and a half, and from St- Thomas to Grenada again. This steamer will land the outward European and intercolonial mails, from Grenada to Curagoa and from Curagoa to Grenada, by Sainana, &c., land and take in intercolonial mails. The return European mails from all the places between Grenada and Samana southwaids will be carried forward by the next "steamer, which bring the mails by the following packet from Europe. From Grenada other steamers will proceed to Saint Vincent's, Saint Lucia, Martinique, Dominica, Guadaloupe, Muntserrat, Antigua,
Nuvis, and St. Kill's, making the passages

LiuaKifT" ' -- .v + m.-. .-.. . - -<. u WJ». CMBM>,' between each Island in from 4 to 13 hours, and touching at the whole in the two days. From St. Kilts to Tor tola and St. Thomas from thence lb Samana by Porto Rico þÿ thence back to Grenada by Curagoa, &.c., making the whole round in 12 days. The chief Haytian mail will be landed at Cape Nichola Mole--from thence a sailing schooner is to take in the mails for Crooked Islands and Nassau, returning in 1 1 days. From Grenada to Samana northwards, (St. Thomas and Portorico excepted) the steamer will land the outward European and intercolonial mails for all the islands eastward, northward, and Westward. The return European mails from the former places, will be carried forward from Grenada to Jamaica by the next steamer, with the mails by the following packet from Europe. All these Islands and places will have fifteen days to reply to letters. From Curagoa, a sailing vessel will carry forward mails to Santa Martha and Cartliagena, and the return mails from these places will be brought by the steamers, which are to leave Jamaica for Chagres direct, and after a stay of 2j days, will return to Jamaica by Carthagena and Santa Martha. At Chagres the outward mails for the Pacific will be landed, and those from Panama brought back. From Savanah-la-mar a sailing vessel will carry forward the outward maiis to Trinidad de Cuba, aud go thence to Beiisle in the Bay of Honduras, and back by the same route, in about 20 days. From Havannah a steamer will proceed to Mobile thence to Tampico, and on to Veia

Cruz, stopping there one day, and making the voyage out and back in 12 days, þÿ another steamer will also be employed on this route, going first to Vera Cruz from Havannah and back by Tampico and Mobile. The next part of the plan, and that which will most deeply interest our readers in the British Colonies, is that which connects the whole of these lines of steam communication, which, like a spider's web are to touch every point of importance, from Guiana to Mobile, (including almost every island in ihe great western Archipelago,) with the northern State of the Union, and the provinces of British America. For this purpose, steamer a is to leave Havannah for New York, touching at Savannah and Charleston, and running the distance of 1200 miles in 0 days; from New York she is to go on to Halifax in three days, so that allowing ten days lor stoppages at New York and Halifax, the voyage from Havannah to Halifax and back will occupy but 28 days, and letters sent either way will reach their destination in nine days certain. þÿ These steamers twice in each month, will be so regulated that they will reach Havannah from New York before the outward steamer arrives from Jamaica, and will leave immediately after her arrival. They are to take in their coals for the voy age at Halifax The boats to be employed are to be built for the purpose, of the same tonnage and power (400), in order that they may all in rotation fall into the great line, arid make the voyage to Europe

KjXSISX THE DUKE OF WELLINGTON AND SIR JAMES MAC DUE' ELL. A friend has related to us an anecdote illustrative not orilv "I the high opinion entertained bv his grace of this distinguished General, but of the delicate generosity displayed by Sir James to a non commissioned officer of his regiment. Some three years ago the Duke of Wellington was waited upon at Apslev House by two gentlemen, who announced to him that, as executors, to the will of a deceased Iriend of eccentric habits, who had left 500 £ to the bravest man in the British Army, they had called for the purpose of handing to his Grace a check tor that amount ; being fully satisfied, that in so doing, they should religiously fulfil the duty imposed on them by the testator. The Duke thanked them for the compliment they had paid him, but resolutely declined to receive the money ; alleging, that the British Army contained many as brave men as himself. After several vain remonstrances, his Grace's visitors earnestly requested, that he would consent to become arbitrator in the matter, and indicate the individual on whom the bequest should he conferred. To this appeal he acceded , promising, in the course of two or three davs. to give the matter his consideration, and report to them the result. At the appointed time they again made their appearance at Apsley-House. The Duke received them with great courtesy: but assured them that he had found the task a great deal more difficult than he had anticipated. Alter enumerating to them the various battles iti which he had been engaged, and some of

the most striking feats of heroism he had witnessed, he suggested, that if they had no objection, he would make his selection from the battle of Waterloo ; that being the last, the greatest, and most important action of the war. This point being adjusted, his Grace proceeded to state, that Hugueinoni having been the key to his entire position, and that post having been defended not only with the most complete success but with the most chivalrous bravery, by Major General Sir James Mac Donell, who commanded there, he could point out no one so fully entitled to the legacy as that officer. The executors repaired accordingly to Sir Jaines Macdonell, and having acquainted him with the decision of the Duke of Wellington, tendered him the money. Sir James expressed himself highly flatn red by so distinguished a mark of his Grace's approval, and observed, that although he should not attempt to dispute altogether the propriety of his decision, yet, as he knew a man who had conducted himself with at least equal gallantry in the same battle, he must insist on sharing the prize with him. He then went on to say, that at one period of the day the French troops rushed upon Huguenriont with such irrestible force, that the gates of the farm were burst open, and, for a moment, the fate of the position appeared doubtful ; when a powerful scrjeant major of the Coldstream Guards, of the name of Frsser, assisted him in closing the gates, which they did, by dint of sheer physical strength, upon the enemy. Shortly after the

French were driven hack with great slaughter. and the fate of lluguemont was decided. Sir James added, that the Duke of Wellington had evidently selected hitn because fie was able to make good a post which was a key to his position ; and he could not, on the same principle, withhold from the gallant soldier who assisted him at so critical a moment iu forcing out the enemy, his proper share of the reward. He would, therefore, accept the 500£. and divide it with Serjeant- Major Frnser, to whom he accordingly paid 25 0£ of the money þÿ United Set nice Gazette.

After the battle between the Chinese and the British at the Cogue, the troops of the latter went to Macao, and took away all the British residents. þÿ The Chinese Admiial had died of his wounds The Commissioner. Lin, had sent an express to Peking, with an account of the battle, and for the purpose of procuring the orders of the Emperor for luturs operation. From the Canton Press, published at M aca<>, Nov. 9ih The Battle between the British and the Ciii ' Esb þÿ Tli« ships of war, the Volage and the Hyacinth, left the Macao roads on the 28th October, and proceeded to the Bogue. Strong northerly winds delayed their arrival there until Saturday morning the 2d November, when Capt. Smith sent a despatch to the Commissioner at Chuenpce, the purport of which was a demand that the Commissioner should withdraw his often repeated threats of burning and destroying the English merchant fleet now at Hong kong. and allow them to remain there unmolested until the orders of the home government had been received, or until other arrangements for the discharge of their cargoes had been made ; that, if these threats were not withdrawn, he Capt. Smith, would he obliged, in defence of the lives and property of h s countrymen, which it was Ins duty to protect, to take effectual measures tor their safety. This chop, having been delivered, the Chinese requested the ships of war to remove some wav farther from the Bogue, and Capt. Smith complied with their wish and dropped down about three miles, waiting for

the replv. On the following morning the despatch was returned, unopened, wc believe, and without an answer, 'and twentynine war junks were seen coming down upon the two ships, when Capt Smith sent again a letter to the Chinese Admiral, warning him not to come to near, as he would he obliged to fire on him in self defence. To this the Admiral returned an answer that he should pioceed as he thought proper, and again deminded the immediate surrender of the murderer of Lin Weihc. Upon this, the junks coming very near with a fair wind and tide, the Volage, we believe, filed a shot across the bows of the þÿAdmiral s slop, w hich was immediately answered with four from (lie Chinese An action was now inevitable, and in less than an þÿhour time, s between twelve and one þÿo clock, the whole of the 29 junks were disabled þÿ llnee had been sunk, one was blown up, several others drifted tin shore in a sinking state, and of many the whole crew had jumped overboard to save themselves by swimming, leaving th«ir vessels at the mercy of wind and tide. The junk in which the Admiral was had been so roughly handled, that the officer, who is represented to have displayed considerable personal courage, left her w hen sinking for another junk, some say badly wounded. The Chinese, though they displayed courage, seem to he very had gunnels, few of their shot having told, and only done some slight damage to the rigging of the Hyacinth. The English had only one man very slightly wounded, nnd though the loss of
(lie Chinese is not known to a c.eitainty, it

Accordingly left Macao early the next morning, for Hong kong whither the Volage also proceeded, leaving the Hyacinth in the roads. ft. is difficult to understand what can have the Chinese to the attack on these two English ships of war except it he a total misconception m ignorance of their strength, and that they relied for success on their great superiority of numbers li is rumored that the admiral gave to the commissioner a verv false estimate of the strength of British ships of war ; he is said to h ive reported that, though it was true jthat the English had laige and very good guns, and that though in point of sailing the English had the advantage over the Chinese, yet, that their ciews were lazy and good ior nothing, lying on dock the whole day either sleeping or smoking, and it would tie an easy thing for two Chinese junks to take one English ship; the junks had only to go alongside, one on each side, then hoard the ship, immediately cut down her masts, make the crew prisoners, who would only be too

glad to beg for their lives, and then destroy the ship I he compliance of captain .'Smith on the previous day with the desire of the Chinese that he should more farther down the river, may probably also h ive been bv tlieru construed into fear, and was possibly one of the causes of the total destruction of the tieci, which came down on the English ships with fair wind and tide, and could therefore, when in danger, not retreat under the batteries of the forts, which have lately been much strengthened, and a new one Imilt with a formidable row of cannon. Upon such accounts and surmises the commissioner is said to have proceeded in ordering the attack on ihe I ohifie and lli/iicinlh , and to he rjiute certain of success, sent the great number of junks wc have mentioned, some of which mounted as many as sixteen guns, and and none, we believe, less than eight : their crews may have numbered between 100 and 200 men each. was kept up until daylight, without however doing i lie slightest damage, not a single ball having hit any of the ships, though some of the shot wore heard to pass ovoi the vessels nearest the land. At day light soldiers P"

weie seeu on the shore removing iri great haste, and the guns seemed also to have been removed, nothing hut the hastily thrown up breastworks remaining. Vo attempt was made from the shipping, though the Hyacinth was at Hongkong, to laud and destroy the forts and batteries, and the fleet remained at anchor all that day and the next night, the weather continuing calm, but on Thursday the greatest part set sail for Tongkoo bay, .and were on the next day followed by the remainder; where they are all now anchored This removal from Hongkong, though it will no doubt be represented by the Chinese as a flight ftotn their cannon, had been previously determined on, in consequence of circulars sent by Capt Smith, of H. M S. Volage, that only at Tungkoo would the merchant ships henceforward enjoy the protection of the ships of war.

We have in these evil times heard much about the probable issue of an attack upon the Celestial Empire.
